hops.afterHeading: One in two thousand: the puzzle
hops.title: Mosquito smell neurons break the one-receptor rule
hops.text: It is tempting to treat one receptor per neuron as a law of smell. Many neurons in Aedes aegypti, the mosquito that spreads dengue, ignore it. When researchers disrupted the shared co-receptor gene Orco, disabling one major smell pathway, female mutants still showed strong attraction to human scent when carbon dioxide was present. In 2022, Herre and colleagues found a possible explanation: many of the mosquito's smell neurons express receptors from different gene families in the same cell. They proposed that this redundancy helps make the mosquito's human detector so hard to break. Singular choice is one way to build a nose, not the only one.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A striped Aedes aegypti mosquito hovering above a pair of worn running sneakers on a sunny wooden porch.
image.caption: Many mosquito smell neurons co-express receptors from different gene families, and tested cells respond to distinct odor classes.

hops.afterHeading: Escaping the silence: enhancer hubs that compete
hops.title: COVID-19 and the smell neurons the virus rarely infects
hops.text: Many people with COVID-19 lost their sense of smell abruptly, yet the virus rarely infects smell neurons. In hamsters, SARS-CoV-2 mainly infects the support cells around them; in human tissue, viral RNA sat mostly in non-neuronal layers. In olfactory tissue from infected hamsters and human autopsies, Zazhytska and colleagues (2022) found less receptor-gene RNA, and separately measured weaker contacts between receptor-gene clusters across chromosomes, including in sorted human smell-neuron nuclei. Serum from infected hamsters, with its virus inactivated, was enough to reduce the contacts; the factor responsible is unidentified. Ten days after infection, contacts remained reduced in hamster olfactory tissue where viral RNA was no longer detectable.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student at a sunlit kitchen table looking puzzled while leaning over a steaming mug of coffee beside an orange and a cinnamon roll.
image.caption: Olfactory tissue from infected hamsters and COVID-19 autopsies showed weaker receptor-cluster contacts and less receptor-gene RNA than controls.

hops.afterHeading: What the choice buys: one pocket
hops.title: Spearmint and caraway: one molecule, two mirror images
hops.text: Sniff a stick of spearmint gum, then a pinch of caraway seeds, the taste of rye bread. Their characteristic scents come from carvone, the same molecule built as left- and right-handed mirror images. The atoms and bonds match, differing only in three-dimensional arrangement, yet people can tell them apart because handed (chiral) receptor pockets can respond differently to each form. Using a model checked with mutants in cells, Geithe and colleagues (2017) identified eleven positions in human receptor OR1A1 that shape how it responds to each form. About eight percent of people are reported unable to smell the spearmint form; OR1A1 is one candidate receptor for that gap.

sources.citation: Geithe et al., Cellular and Molecular Life Sciences (2017), PMID: 28656349

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A student seen from behind leaning over a kitchen counter to sniff a stick of spearmint gum, caraway seeds and rye bread.
image.caption: Spearmint and caraway smell different because mirror-image carvone molecules fit receptor pockets differently.

audio.title: Cloned noses, elephant pseudogenes and a floral gene
audio.transcript:
Three true stories about olfactory receptor choice outside the textbook diagram. First, how did biologists test whether a permanent change in D N A locks in a smell neuron's receptor choice? Developing B cells cut and rejoin stretches of their D N A to build the genes for their antibody chains. For years, people wondered whether olfactory neurons did something similar to fix their one receptor out of a thousand. In two thousand four, two research teams tested the idea directly: they lifted the nucleus from a mature mouse olfactory neuron, already committed to a single receptor, transferred it into an egg whose own nucleus had been removed, and used the resulting embryonic stem cells to produce cloned mice. One group took neurons expressing a receptor called M seventy-one. If choice had made a permanent D N A change that locked the genome into the donor's receptor choice, the descendants should have been stuck with M seventy-one alone. Instead, the cloned mice showed normal receptor patterns in the tests the teams ran, smell neurons descended from an M seventy-one neuron could express other receptors, and the team found no D N A rearrangement at the M seventy-one gene. A smell neuron can make a lasting choice without permanently rearranging its D N A. In mice, chromatin keeps receptor genes quiet early on, hubs help a winner emerge, and feedback from the receptor protein helps keep that choice stable.

Second, that feedback lock deals with an awkward mess hiding inside mammalian genomes: broken genes. In two thousand fourteen, researchers cataloged odorant receptor genes across thirteen placental mammals and found an unexpected record holder. The survey counted one thousand nine hundred forty-eight intact odorant receptor genes in the African elephant, about one point seven times the mouse count and roughly five times the human count. Right beside those working genes sit two thousand two hundred thirty broken pseudogenes, more duds than working receptors. Guinea pigs carry an even bigger share of broken ones, around sixty-two percent. Just over half the receptor genes in the elephant survey are pseudogenes. So how would a developing neuron recover if it happened to pick one? Mouse experiments point to an escape route. When a coding deletion or frameshift stops the chosen gene from making a receptor that supplies feedback, the neuron can switch on a second receptor gene instead. Neurons with a broken receptor switch far more often than neurons with a working one.

Third, once a neuron settles on its winner, that one receptor shapes what dinner smells like. Consider beta-ionone, an aroma molecule found in many foods and drinks and added to give a pleasant floral note. Some people pick it up at tiny traces, while someone sitting right next to them barely notices it. In two thousand thirteen, researchers in New Zealand traced that gap to a single amino acid substitution in one human receptor, O R five A one. In the study, that one variant correctly predicted who fell into the more or less sensitive group for just over ninety-six percent of participants, so sensitivity behaved almost like a classic single-gene trait. Participants with the sensitive version described test foods with added beta-ionone, such as chocolate, as fragrant or floral, and the variant also went with differences in which offered samples they chose. A single amino acid change in one of your roughly four hundred smell receptors can turn the same snack into two different experiences.
